extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and mathematics researchers (graduate students, postdocs, faculty) writing research papers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for clear communication and organization when writing mathematical research papers: how to write the introduction, structure sections and lemmas, give citations, choose level of detail, and present assumptions and proofs so readers can follow the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get to the point quickly (Introduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Get to the point, quickly. Attention is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sell the key points in the introduction; prioritize brevity and immediacy to capture limited reader attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: State main results in appropriate detail
rubrics_metrics.description: State main results in appropriate detail. Consider writing a special case of your main theorem before stating it in full generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present a clear statement of the main theorem(s); when helpful, give a special-case or simpler version first so readers understand the core idea before the full generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain new aspects and consequences relative to literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain new aspects, merits, consequences of your main results by comparison to existing work in the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear what is new and why it matters by contrasting with prior results; this helps readers place your contribution in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citations: include full author list and year
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing other papers, write all the authors’ names, not just something like “[4]”. Also, write the year, always.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including authors' names and years helps both advanced and new researchers form a coherent story; consider embedding year in citation marks (e.g., “[F77]”) and automate via LaTeX settings where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss sharpness and possible hypothesis removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Can one drop hypotheses in the main results and still have true statements? Are there relevant counterexamples showing the “sharpness” of your results? Give these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address whether assumptions are necessary and supply counterexamples or remarks that demonstrate sharpness; this clarifies the scope and limits of theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide hierarchical signposting and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader only knows the structure of your argument if you tell them. Authors must provide hierarchical structure with plenty of signposting text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because authors suffer from the ‘curse of knowledge’, explicitly explain relationships among definitions, lemmas, and theorems, and how parts fit into the overall argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sections should be major milestones and have informative titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections of the paper should be major milestones for your results. If a title like “Step 2” is the only possible name for a section, then you should reorganize the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use informative section titles (e.g., “Counting polynomial configurations”, “Proof of Theorem 1.1: Small arcs”) and avoid generic titles like “Technical lemmas.” Minimize the use of math symbols in titles. Apply the “Step 2 test” to judge section worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a roadmap/outline in the introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the major milestones in the introduction, perhaps in a little subsection called “Roadmap,” “Structure,” or “Outline.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A short roadmap helps readers understand the flow of the paper and the roles of the main sections before diving into technical details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a logical-dependency map
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a map explaining the implications and logical dependencies of the results of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the handful of key results and how they depend on lesser results; include the map if it clarifies non-linear dependencies (avoid if the structure is trivially linear like A→B→C). The act of making the map clarifies paper milestones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay or hide less important content
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggressively hide less important content. Side remarks, tedious computations, and overly technical proofs should be delayed as much as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place technical or peripheral material later in the paper so early readers are not distracted; delaying increases the chance readers stay engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer later normal sections over appendices for important technical material
rubrics_metrics.description: Yuval adds: Don’t use appendices; instead, use normal sections, just placed later. Don’t look down on your own work by calling it “technical.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If technical parts are central or innovative, integrate them into the paper as later sections rather than relegating to an appendix; label and present them so their importance is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make each section convey one memorable result
rubrics_metrics.description: If possible, each section should be summarizable in one result. Ask whether the reader can safely forget everything except one result from the section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design sections so they have one clear takeaway, which helps readers retain the core contributions even if they forget details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only state lemmas that are psychologically important or reused
rubrics_metrics.description: If you state a lemma, it should be psychologically important or used more than once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key subarguments used multiple times merit lemmas; minor subarguments used once may be folded into proofs. Note: Yuval argues for a modular structure instead (give each step its own lemma) to help readers check parts separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rewriting proofs of standard lemmas without reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rewrite proofs of standard lemmas without a good reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite well-known results rather than reproving them; if the canonical source is inaccessible or outdated, consider rewriting in modern language and note this explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give precise references (point to propositions/sections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give precise references to cited works. For example, instead of referring to an entire book, refer to Proposition 7.1 in the book instead; same for papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for a good, citable source for “well known” results; consult peers if needed. Precise references help readers verify claims efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make statements of lemmas and theorems self-contained
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements of lemmas and theorems should be self-contained: all of the terms in the result are defined in the paper, and all additional assumptions are stated in the text of the theorem or lemma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hidden global assumptions that are easy to miss. For long or repeated assumptions, use numbered assumptions (e.g., “Assumption (1)”) or state a lemma once with full assumptions and later lemmas as 'Let f be as in Lemma 3.1.' This increases clarity for non-linear readers.
